title: The Moment It Becomes Chips
description:
The cashier's cage at Jeongseon Casino.

{name} slid the cash across. The clerk counted it, then pushed back a stack of chips.

Green, black, purple. They had weight.

Strange. What was money a second ago felt like toys in his hand.
50,000 won per chip. The fact that a chip WAS 50,000 won — it didn't register.

That was the game's first trick, {name} would realize later.

choices.text: Exchange only what he decided beforehand
choices.result_text:
Only 100,000 won worth. Left the wallet in the car.

Two chips. That's all there is today.
Lose it, he's done. Win, he gets up. Setting the rule in advance made his mind lighter.

The lighter the chips look, the more the person who sets a limit wins.

choices.text: Exchange plenty — running short kills the mood
choices.result_text:
Got 300,000 won in chips. Heavy.

He figured having plenty meant playing with peace of mind.
But that 'plenty' quickly became the baseline. 300,000 had somehow become 'today's spending money.'

That the more you exchange, the more you lose — no one at the cashier's cage tells you that.

title: A Room With No Clocks
description:
Feels like he's been playing a while, but he can't tell the time.

{name} scanned the walls. No clocks.
No windows either. No way to tell if it was day or night outside.

The lighting, always the same brightness. The air, always the same temperature.
A waiter brought a drink. It was free.

In here, everyone had silently agreed to pretend time wasn't passing.

choices.text: Check the time on his phone and get up
choices.result_text:
4:17 AM.

{name} gathered his chips and stood. His legs were numb. He'd been sitting six hours.

The cold air hit his face when he stepped out. Dawn in the mountains.
He welcomed that cold. Time had started flowing again.

Walking out of a room with no clocks on your own two feet — that was a skill too.

choices.text: One more game — the time to quit is after a win
choices.result_text:
'I'll end it on a win.' And so another hour passed.

Then another. Win and you want more, lose and you want it back.
The time to quit was structurally designed to never arrive.

When he came to, five empty glasses were stacked beside him.
A room with no clocks also makes the exit hard to find.

title: A Free Room
description:
Someone who looked like a manager approached.

"Sir, you've enjoyed yourself today. Shall I arrange a hotel room for you? Breakfast included, on the house."

Polite. Kind. Treating {name} like a VIP.

For a moment it felt good — then {name} caught himself.

Giving you a free room meant: be here tomorrow too.

choices.text: "No thanks, I'll catch the last bus" — decline
choices.result_text:
"Appreciate it, but I have to head out."

The manager handed over a business card. "Call anytime." Smiling.

{name} walked to the bus terminal. The last bus was tight.

There's always a reason behind what's given for free. Walking the opposite way from that reason — that was today's victory.

choices.text: "Just one night, then…" — accept the favor
choices.result_text:
The room was nice. The view was nice.

But he couldn't sleep. Staring at the ceiling, thinking about tomorrow's table.

In the morning he ate breakfast and, naturally, exchanged chips again.
The real price of the free room showed up in his account at checkout.

Nothing in this world is free. The casino, especially.

title: A Stranger's All-In
description:
A noise came from the next table.

A man in his late thirties pushed all his chips in. All-in.
His hands were shaking. He'd been losing for a while.

The opponent called. The cards turned over.

The man lost. He stared at the cards a long time, then slowly stood.
Said nothing. Just grabbed his jacket and climbed the stairs.

{name} watched him go. It was a familiar back.

choices.text: Call it a night — that could be my future
choices.result_text:
{name} cashed out his remaining chips.

The man's shaking hands kept coming back to him. Could be himself in a year, in five years.

Climbing the stairs, he resolved: this place looks like somewhere you 'win on skill,'
but in the end it's a place where the one who stands up last wins.

Today, he stood up. That was enough.

choices.text: Not my problem — I'd never do that
choices.result_text:
{name} turned his eyes back to the cards. That guy had no self-control, and he was different.

He focused on the next hand. He believed he could control himself.

'I'm different.' The man who climbed those stairs probably thought so too, at first.
That fact didn't surface that night.

title: What the Table Taught Him
description:
A negotiation at work. Or an interview. Or a meeting with a client.

Wherever it was, he caught himself reading the face across from him.

Is this person holding a strong hand and acting tough, or bluffing with a weak one?
He watched the hands more than the words, the eyes more than the hands.

It was an instinct honed at the holdem table.

{name} suddenly wondered: what if he'd used this skill somewhere else?

choices.text: Use that instinct for work — cut back on the table
choices.result_text:
{name} stayed one beat calmer in negotiations.

How to make the other side show their hand first. How to hide his own.
He'd paid steep tuition at the table to learn that.

Now he decided to recoup that tuition outside the table.
His trips to the holdem club dropped. His bank balance rose instead.

choices.text: The table really is the most honest — go more often
choices.result_text:
The table was more comfortable than the office. There, doing well got you chips right away.

{name} grew slowly accustomed to that structure of instant effort-and-reward.

Reality was slow, the table was fast.
That gap in speed is how it slowly breaks a person — he didn't know that yet.

title: The Old Man's Real Story
description:
Gwacheon. The racetrack man had a bit of drink in him today.

"Back in my day, you know." He smiled. But his eyes didn't.

"I had a house. In Anyang. Two kids, too."

{name} listened quietly.

"Twenty years here. At first I came for fun, like you. But there were days I won. I can't forget the feeling of those days. That's the problem."

He folded his racing paper. "Take it easy, kid. Don't end up like me."

choices.text: "Let's leave together today" — walk out with him
choices.result_text:
{name} dragged the old man out. The two went to a gukbap place.

The old man said it'd been a while since he went home without betting.
"Thanks, kid." He smiled awkwardly.

On the way back, {name} thought: that man's twenty-years-ago could be me.
Just having heard that story — today wasn't a wasted trip.

choices.text: Sad, but — still watch the race today
choices.result_text:
The old man's story was sad. But {name} bought a ticket today anyway.

'I'm not that far gone.' That distance was a comfort.

He lost 30,000 won and caught the last train.
Staring out the window, he heard the "don't end up like me" again.
It sounded like a warning sent back from the future. He pretended not to hear it.

title: The Last Race, the Last People
description:
The final race of the day.

The betting window was unusually crowded. {name} joined the line.

The man ahead was counting ten-thousand won bills. His hands shook. Only a few left.
The man behind was muttering. "This time for real… this time it has to hit."

The last race is left with only the people trying to win back what they lost today.

{name} was one of them in that line.

choices.text: Step out of the line — he knows where it ends
choices.result_text:
{name} stepped out of the line.

Everyone in that line had the same face. Desperate, exhausted, believing in one big hit.
That face scared him because it looked like his own.

He walked to the station without betting. The last train was empty.
Going home without winning it back. That was harder than winning it back.

choices.text: Last one, so bet big — a chance to recover
choices.result_text:
{name} bet everything he'd lost today. Because it was the last one.

The horses ran. He watched to the end. It wasn't it.

The betting window was empty by then. Everyone scattered with the same expression.

On the last train he opened his banking app. Chasing the loss had doubled it in a day.
The phrase 'last race' was dangerous precisely because it was never the last.
